summary: An island country in the Leeward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, made up of the islands of Antigua and Barbuda, which became independent from Britain in 1981 and is known for its claim of 365 beaches.

ranking.name: Anglicanism
ranking.description: Anglicanism arrived when the English founded a colony in Antigua in 1632, and in the colonial period it was the official church; most sugar plantation owners and colonial officials were Anglicans. After the abolition of slavery in 1834, the Anglican Church also preached to the freed residents of African descent, and it remains the largest denomination today; St. John's Cathedral is a landmark of the capital.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church was brought to the British Caribbean by American missionaries at the end of the 19th century, and from the 20th century it grew rapidly in Antigua through schools, medical care and the promotion of healthy diets. It observes the Saturday Sabbath and has considerable influence among the lower and middle classes and in rural communities.

ranking.name: Pentecostalism
ranking.description: Pentecostalism was introduced in the mid to late 20th century from the United States and other Caribbean islands, attracting believers with fervent worship, speaking in tongues and faith healing. After independence in 1981, social openness and the influence of American religious media have kept it expanding, and its share is now comparable to that of the Seventh-day Adventists.

ranking.name: Moravian Church
ranking.description: The Moravian Church is a Protestant denomination that originated in Bohemia; its missionaries came to Antigua in 1756, and it was one of the earliest churches to preach specifically to Black slaves and teach them to read and write. Because it stood on the side of the slaves during the era of slavery, it left a deep foundation in the African-descended community.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was long a minority under British colonial rule, and from the 19th century it grew with Portuguese immigrants from Madeira, the Irish, and migrants from neighboring French islands. In recent years Spanish-speaking immigrants from the Dominican Republic and elsewhere have also increased the number of Catholics.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The share of the non-religious population is not high, and consists mainly of young people who are highly educated or have lived overseas. Antiguan society as a whole still attaches considerable importance to religion, and churches play an important role in community life, so only about 6 percent identify as having no religion.

religion.background: The indigenous peoples of Antigua were the Arawaks and the Caribs; Columbus named the island in 1493, and the English began colonizing it in 1632. The colonists established sugar plantations and imported large numbers of African slaves; the Anglican Church became the official church, while the Moravian Church and the Methodists began preaching to slaves from the 18th century, so that Christianity took root among residents of African descent. After abolition in 1834, the various Protestant denominations played an important role in education and social services. From the 20th century the Seventh-day Adventists and Pentecostals grew rapidly, forming today's pattern of coexisting denominations.

ranking.name: English (including Antiguan Creole)
ranking.description: English arrived with British colonization in 1632 and is the official language used by the government, schools and the media. In daily life most people speak Antiguan Creole, which formed in the plantation era from a mixture of the languages of West African slaves and English; its vocabulary mostly comes from English, but its grammar and pronunciation retain West African features. Because the two are closely related, censuses usually combine them, and about 95 percent of the population use them.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish speakers are mainly immigrants who came from the Dominican Republic after the 1980s, along with some residents from Venezuela, Cuba and elsewhere. Most work in services and domestic work, forming a small Spanish-speaking community.

language.history: The indigenous languages of Antigua before colonization disappeared along with the indigenous peoples and no longer exist. From 1632 the English colonized the island and the plantations imported large numbers of West African slaves; through contact with the English they formed Antiguan Creole, which became the everyday language of residents of African descent. English has always been the language of administration and education of the colony and remained the official language after independence in 1981. Because Creole was long regarded as 'non-standard English' and schools taught only in English, scholars have only in recent years begun to promote recognition of the cultural value of Creole.

ranking.name: Fungee and Pepperpot
ranking.description: Smooth cornmeal paste cooked with okra (fungee), served with a thick spicy stew of meat, spinach, eggplant and pumpkin.
ranking.history: Fungee with pepperpot is regarded as the national dish of Antigua and Barbuda. The method of making fungee is similar to the pasty staples made from corn or cassava in West Africa and is a food tradition that slaves brought from Africa; in the plantation era, cornmeal was the main ration issued to slaves by the colonists. The dish is especially common around Independence Day on 1 November and is regarded as a symbol of national culture.

ranking.name: Pepperpot
ranking.description: A thick green stew of salted pork or beef cooked for a long time with spinach, eggplant, okra, pumpkin and peas; it is salty, savory and slightly spicy.
ranking.history: Antiguan pepperpot differs from the 'pepperpot' of Guyana and elsewhere, which stews meat in cassava juice, and is closer to West African leafy-vegetable stews. In the plantation era, slaves used the salted meat they were allotted and the vegetables from their own gardens to cook a pot that could be kept for a long time. Cooking pepperpot on Saturdays is a habit of many Antiguan families, and it is usually eaten with fungee.

ranking.name: Ducana
ranking.description: Sweet dumplings made by mixing mashed sweet potato, shredded coconut, flour, sugar and spices, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed, often eaten with saltfish.
ranking.history: Ducana is similar in name to the 'dokono' (fermented corn dough) of Ghana in West Africa, and it is generally thought to derive from the leaf-wrapped steamed food tradition brought by African slaves. Sweet potatoes and coconuts grow easily in the Caribbean and became important foods for slaves in the plantation era. Today ducana with saltfish is a traditional Sunday breakfast or lunch in Antigua.

ranking.name: Saltfish
ranking.description: Salted cod is soaked in water to remove the salt, shredded, and stir-fried with onion, tomato and sweet pepper; it is often eaten for breakfast with ducana, fungee or bread.
ranking.history: Salt cod is native to the North Atlantic, and in the 17th and 18th centuries merchants of New England and Newfoundland in Canada shipped cheap, long-lasting salt fish to the Caribbean in exchange for sugar and rum, so that salt fish became the source of protein that plantation owners allotted to slaves. The history of this 'triangular trade' remains on today's dinner tables, and saltfish dishes are very common throughout the English-speaking Caribbean.

ranking.name: Antigua Black Pineapple
ranking.description: A small pineapple variety unique to Antigua, with dark green, almost black skin and golden flesh that is high in sweetness and low in acidity, and can be eaten raw.
ranking.history: The pineapple is native to South America, and it is generally thought that the indigenous Arawaks brought the pineapple to Antigua before colonization. The 'Antigua Black pineapple' already enjoyed a reputation in the British colonial period, and in the 18th century British aristocrats regarded the pineapple as a luxury. Today it is one of Antigua's national symbols, with a pineapple design on the coat of arms, and it is grown mainly in the southwest of the island.
